motion: After Gaza, Arab unity is dead and buried.

dropped_turns.speaker: PRO
dropped_turns.text: No, those ties do not make unity alive; they show people compensate for its collapse. Your wounded-not-buried point avoids the motion: Gaza revealed no reliable collective force when it mattered.

dropped_turns.speaker: CON
dropped_turns.text: Your 'reliable force' point sets a standard no living community always meets. Unity can weaken and recover; the continuing shared response proves burial is the wrong word.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Welcome. Today's motion is: After Gaza, Arab unity is dead and buried. Paula argues for the motion, and Benjamin argues against it. Each opening is thirty seconds, followed by two and a half minutes of crossfire, then thirty-second closings; I will give a ten-second cue. Keep remarks direct, address each other, and wait for recognition before speaking.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Gaza did not merely reveal disagreement. It showed governments choosing separate priorities, separate messages, and separate limits, leaving ordinary people with no common protection.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: No common protection? People across-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Could you let her speak.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Leaving ordinary people with no common protection, while each government calculates its own risk, is exactly what burial looks like: a label remains, but joint power disappears.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds from this side?

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Shared grief matters, but it cannot replace coordinated choices, mutual obligations, or a common direction.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: All right. Benjamin, do you want to come back on that?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: My opponent mistakes fractured leadership for a dead people. Unity is not one command center; it is a continuing capacity to recognize shared harm and press shared demands. Gaza has made those bonds painful and visible, even when governments fail to match them.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: And that concludes round one. Now onto round two and round two is where the debaters address one another. Two and a half minutes on the clock, starting the moment I stop talking.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: You call public feeling a capacity, but feeling cannot protect anyone without common decisions. If governments choose separate limits when Gaza demands action, what unity remains beyond a slogan?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: What remains is a shared refusal to treat Gaza as someone else's pain. You assume unity requires identical governments, but solidarity can coordinate pressure, aid, and memory without one ruler.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: When leaders must respond together to a crisis, unity needs common action, not parallel speeches. Gaza created that test, and separate calculations showed the alliance cannot carry a shared burden.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your test assumes unity only counts when leaders act identically. If people organize help and keep demanding a common stand, why declare their unity dead because officials hesitate to move-

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Because help is humane, not proof of a durable political union. You are replacing unity with sympathy; sympathy can fill a room, yet governments still abandon each other when decisions matter.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Families also need food, shelter, and safe routes, and arguing over leaders can hide that urgency. Still, the motion concerns unity, and shared care across borders shows it endures.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Unity cannot be declared alive by scattered acts of care when common action is required. A people facing the same wound still lacks unity if its collective power never arrives.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your claim ignores the bonds that make collective power possible. Every Arab summit shows unity still lives. Leaders may disappoint, but the forum, shared language, and repeated return to Gaza keep cooperation alive.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Your 'every summit' point confuses gathering with unity. A room can meet while members protect incompatible interests; Gaza has turned repeated meetings into evidence that shared words do not produce shared resolve.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: At an emergency summit, leaders offered divided words and no shared course. This Arab summit shows unity does not live. Their inability to agree proves leadership is failing, not that people are divided.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: But doesn't your argument for every Arab summit shows unity still lives fight your argument that this Arab summit shows unity does not live?

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: I stand by both statements. The continuing forum shows unity survives as a bond, while this summit shows that bond failed to guide leaders; survival is not the same as strength.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Imagine neighboring governments watching a family flee, each refusing entry until another acts. The family remains trapped between promises. That is the harm of dead unity: shared identity without shared responsibility.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds left in the crossfire.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Your trapped-family example condemns governments, not unity itself. Neighbors who argue over entry-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: That's time. So, let's move on to round three and our closing statements on the resolution after Gaza, Arab unity is dead and buried. Making her closing statement, here is Paula.

turns.speaker: PRO
turns.text: Benjamin's best point is that shared grief and help are real. But grief without binding action leaves each government free to walk away at the decisive moment. Gaza exposed that gap again and again, so Arab unity is not merely weak; it is dead and buried.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Let's take that to Benjamin, please.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: Paula is right that leaders have failed people at decisive moments. Yet she treats failure as a grave, when it can become a demand for renewal. My strongest point is simple: unity lives in shared recognition and repeated cooperation, not perfect obedience. People still organize care, speak, and insist that suffering belongs to all of them. Insistence matters because

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Ten seconds, Benjamin.

turns.speaker: CON
turns.text: it refuses the story that separate leaders erase a shared people. A buried thing cannot answer pain, but people still answer it together, and that living-

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry. Hit time.

turns.speaker: MOD
turns.text: Thank you, Paula and Benjamin, for a vigorous debate. This concludes our discussion of the motion this evening.
